articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet for Their First Summit: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Meet for Their First Summit: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down for a meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday — a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.
All three made brief opening statements before meeting behind closed doors for about an hour and a half. The leaders did not offer joint or separate statements to reporters after the sit-down, and Mr. Trump immediately left for the airport to return home.
Putin's senior aid Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it said was a statement jointly agreed on by all three leaders characterizing the talks.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the Kremlin readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the Russian government said the leaders had "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House did not offer an immediate readout of the meeting, but indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
He said he intended to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence.
The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.
"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."
Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.
Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.
During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has met with his Chinese and Russian counterparts for highly anticipated trilateral talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ( APEC ) summit.
Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin met for a “family photo” before convening for talks on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in an unprecedented gathering of the world’s three superpowers.
Opening the meeting, Xi said that it “has groundbreaking significance”.
“The world is at peace when great powers live in harmony,” Xi said, adding that the three countries “should work together to address global challenges”.
In a major statement, the Chinese leader also said “nuclear weapons should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed, building a nuclear-free world,” reported China’s Xinhua news agency.
In Trump’s opening remarks, the US president said the three countries were “uniquely positioned” to discuss nuclear weapons.
“Too often past leaders avoided talking to leaders they had disagreements with,” he said. “No peace ever forged by declining opportunities.”
Meanwhile, in his opening remarks, Putin made it clear that the war in Ukraine would be the focus of his conversation, before the three retreated into closed-door talks which lasted for about 55 minutes.
The talks between the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers were not likely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But the meeting had unnerved smaller countries that feared their interests might be disregarded.
Ahead of the trilateral gathering, Trump held separate bilateral meetings with both Xi and Putin on Thursday.
The US president described Xi as a “friend” and said Washington and Beijing enjoyed a “special relationship”.
“As long as the two of us are in charge, I don’t think we’ll have a problem,” Trump said in opening remarks at his meeting with the Chinese leader. He also boasted that “no other countries can do what we can”.
Trump said the US has done “amazing” things in the past two years, since he returned to power, while praising China for many of its gains over several years.
Xi, meanwhile, said that he remained committed to working with Trump to steer ties between their countries on the “correct course”.
Relations between Beijing and Washington have been stable and improving, Xi said to Trump at the start of their third one-on-one meeting this year, which lasted for about an hour.
“We have established a new definition of a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, giving it new substance based on respect, fairness and reciprocity,” Xi said.
Ahead of the bilateral meeting, Trump said the Board of Trade that he and the Chinese president agreed to form at their Beijing summit in May has brought balance to the two countries’ relationship. He said the US and China had split their tariffs in a “fair way”.
Earlier in the day, during talks with Putin, Trump also called the Russian leader a “friend”.
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this,” Trump told Putin.
A video published by the White House showed the two leaders shaking hands and Trump briefly whispering to Putin at the start of their meeting.
In another video posted by the White House Rapid Response X account, Trump was shown pointing at Putin and saying, “He’s my friend.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the two leaders “discussed the conflict in Ukraine and bilateral relations issues”.
“The meeting between the Russian and US leaders went well,” Ushakov said, according to Russia’s state news agency TASS, adding that Putin left the talks “in an excellent” mood.
Thursday also features the main event of the APEC summit, as representatives of the 21 Pacific Rim economies gather for discussions that will include high-stakes diplomacy, Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu said, reporting from Shenzhen.
“Xi Jinping, who spoke at the banquet last night during the opening ceremony, said the discussion will centre on promoting mutual openness, innovation-driven growth and results-oriented cooperation,” said Yu.
On the US-China-Russia talks, James Bays, Al Jazeera’s diplomatic editor, said that when it comes to Trump, “his personal role always matters to him”.
But, he added, “something worth bearing in mind: you have three leaders here, Trump, Xi, and Putin. Putin has been in power; he’s been in the main driving seat in Moscow for 26 years; Xi’s been there for 14 years; and they know President Trump only has 26 more months.”
Speaking to Fox News earlier on Thursday, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival. Xi greeted Air Force One on the airport tarmac on Wednesday, which contrasted with the more muted greetings offered to other leaders.
“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral summit.
Trump has insisted that nuclear arms control be a central topic of the meeting, despite Beijing’s repeated objections to talks on the issue with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

articles.title_orig: UN’s top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: UN’s top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
The United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague delivered its judgement on Thursday about the military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 mainly Muslim Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
It is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court. The ruling marked only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
The case was brought by the West African nation of The Gambia, which in 2019 accused Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people. It asked the ICJ to rule that Myanmar breached the 1948 Genocide Convention, order it to end any illegal activities targeting the Rohingya and ensure those responsible for genocide are punished.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
Evidence shows Myanmar forces killed 10,000 Rohingya, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya ⁠⁠civilians, perpetrated widespread acts ⁠⁠of sexual violence as well as acts of ⁠⁠extreme violence against children and ⁠⁠attacked fleeing Rohingya ⁠⁠as they sought to flee in large numbers to ‌‌Bangladesh,” he added.
In specific cases that he referred to, he said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include: Facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
The court established that at least four genocidal acts have been proven, said Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen, reporting from the Hague. They are the mass killing of civilians; the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people; serious harm inflicted upon the group; and the prevention of birth.
The Rohingya have long been treated as second-class citizens, well before 2017, according to the judge, Vaessen said. They were also forced to take part in a birth control programme, she added.
“So the judge really saw this as a very strong explanation that … a genocidal act was committed there.”
The verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya,” our correspondent said. “They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US agree to UN reforms, reducing nuclear risks; no major breakthroughs
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US agree to UN reforms, reducing nuclear risks; no major breakthroughs
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said the U.S., Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to reduce the world's nuclear weapons stockpile during his historic trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in opening remarks.
"The power is unbelievable, unthinkable," he said, adding that it's "a very hard thing" for countries to reduce nuclear weapons.
That would include not letting Iran have nuclear weapons, Trump said.
He said the three leaders would also discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine, and criticized "rogue globalist organizations," including the International Criminal Court.
The closely watched meeting ended about an hour and a half after it kicked off late Thursday afternoon, following a working lunch between Trump and Xi that started at least an hour later than originally planned.
Trump told Xi and Putin they were "really making history" with the first-ever trilateral meeting between the the three countries' leaders.
He said it was an "honor" to be at the meeting with Putin and Xi, whom he congratulated on a very successful APEC summit."
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump added. "We feel the opposite."
At the trilateral, Xi said that for large nations, having good interactions is not a choice but a necessity, according to a translation by state media.
In the report, Xi noted China's partnership with Russia, work towards constructive strategic stability in U.S. relations, and called on the three countries to respond to the world's challenges.
Xi laid out four "correct" ways for large countries to interact: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and adherence to dialogue, according to state media.
The Chinese president echoed Trump's comments on nuclear weapons, calling for such arms to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, adding that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
Putin said Russia, China and the U.S. can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, calling for the three leaders to discuss energy security and global and regional issues — including the war in Ukraine.
Beijing only confirmed the closely watched meeting on Monday. The three leaders had briefly gathered Wednesday evening as part of a welcome banquet for the APEC leaders more broadly.

articles.title_orig: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.title_zh: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.content_orig:
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.
In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.
A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.
Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.
Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles. From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplies its troops in southern Ukraine.
Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."
The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.
The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.
It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.
Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.
Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.
The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.
In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".
But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.
Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

articles.title_orig: Major KFC franchisee files for bankruptcy, puts 84 restaurants up for sale
articles.title_zh: Major KFC franchisee files for bankruptcy, puts 84 restaurants up for sale
articles.content_orig:
California Pizza Kitchen co-founder Rick Rosenfield told Fox News Digital how two former prosecutors built a pizza empire and how he believes the iconic chain is moving towards a 'new glory.'
A major KFC franchise operator has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection as declining sales, mounting debt and a dispute over unpaid franchise fees threaten its restaurant operations.
Tasty Chick’n, LLC, a Plano, Texas-based franchisee operating 84 KFC and KFC/Taco Bell locations across 10 states, filed for bankruptcy protection on Nov. 16 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas.
The company, which employs approximately 1,646 workers, is seeking to sell its restaurants through a court-supervised process, according to a declaration filed by President and CEO Thomas Scott.
Tasty Chick’n has struggled with falling sales and shrinking profit margins. Restaurant sales declined approximately 15.6% over three years, while profit margins fell from 11.8% in fiscal 2023 to 4% so far in fiscal 2026.
MCDONALD'S BRINGS BACK MACAULAY CULKIN FOR ‘HOME ALONE’ MEAL WITH A PIZZA TWIST
A Yum! Brands Inc. Kentucky Fried Chicken (KFC) restaurant stands in Norwell, Massachusetts, on Thursday, July 25, 2019. (Scott Eisen/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The financial strain led the operator to defer franchise royalty payments in mid-2025 before largely stopping payments that November.
KFC and Taco Bell subsequently issued a notice of default in December 2025, followed by a September 2026 notice of intent to terminate the company's franchise agreements.
Miami, Florida, Miami International Airport, airport terminal, KFC, Kentucky Fried Chicken fast food restaurant. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images / Getty Images)
The franchisors claimed Tasty Chick’n owed approximately $15.7 million in unpaid royalties, advertising contributions and other fees, according to the bankruptcy filing.
Losing those agreements would prevent the operator from running its restaurants under the KFC and Taco Bell brands, potentially eliminating the business's value as an operating enterprise, Scott said.
KFC’s next-generation restaurant concepts are designed to create more modern, dynamic and hospitality-driven experiences for guests around the world. (KFC / Fox News)
The franchisee also reported approximately $67.2 million in debt owed to lenders led by MidCap Financial Trust, along with more than $2 million in claims tied to unpaid rent and other lease charges.
The company operates 75 standalone KFC restaurants and nine co-branded KFC/Taco Bell locations, with Florida and Tennessee accounting for 45 of its restaurants.

Tasty Chick’n began marketing its restaurants to potential buyers before filing for bankruptcy and is pursuing a sale of the entire business or individual markets, subject to court approval and required franchise consents.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu Associates Acknowledge Role in Setting Off Election Day Arrests
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing calls from lawmakers for an investigation following a report that alleged that a member of his staff provided information to police against Arab citizens in an attempt to influence last month’s elections. The claims, which Netanyahu’s office denies, were made on an Israeli TV news show this weekend.
The controversy centers on the widely publicized arrest of three activists from the Arab party Raam in southern Israel early on the morning of the October 27 election over an alleged cash-for-votes scheme. Throughout the day, Netanyahu and his Likud party repeatedly amplified the arrests to mobilize their own voters, alleging Raam was trying to “steal the elections.”
Courts later rejected police requests to keep the suspects in custody, saying that the arrests were carried out without a valid search or arrest warrant. All suspects have since then been released.
According to an investigation by Channel 12’s “Uvda,” the allegation originated in Netanyahu’s office. The day before the elections, the report alleges, Netanyahu’s chief of staff, Ido Norden, bypassed standard reporting channels and personally contacted the police commissioner to alert him about the activists, passing on information.
Norden allegedly referred police to a separate source who was said to hold information about the activists. But the source was a former employee of the Prime Minister’s Office, the report said.
Based on Norden’s complaint and the information provided by the former employee, police carried out the arrests on election day, the report alleged.
The head of Israel’s Central Elections Committee said in a statement Tuesday that “there is no evidence of election bribery paid to voters on a scale that could affect the election results.” The committee said the investigation into the “many suspicions” raised by the allegations was ongoing, but the effort had shifted to “security related aspects … which are not at the core of the election process and its results.”
On Monday evening, Israel’s Attorney General said she would hold a discussion on the transfer of information from the Prime Minister’s Office to the police. “As part of the discussion, all aspects relating to the matter will be examined,” the Attorney General’s spokesperson said in a statement.
Netanyahu’s office strongly denied the Channel 12 report, saying it was “false and grounds for libel,” but confirmed that Nordan had passed information to the police.
“Criminal information reached Chief of Staff Ido Norden, he fulfilled his duty as expected of any law-abiding citizen and connected that person to the police,” his office said in a statement Sunday evening. Norden learned on the morning of the elections that a person “was indeed caught with tens of thousands of shekels in cash and Raam slips,” the statement continued, referring to a suspect who had already been released.
In a statement, Israel Police said it would examine “the decision-making processes, the chain of reporting, the working interfaces between the relevant police units, and the division of responsibility” related to the allegations in the Channel 12 report. “All police actions, including the operation carried out on election morning, were taken out of commitment and transparency toward the public, and with the aim of protecting the integrity of the elections,” police said.
On Monday evening, the Attorney General requested a pause in this examination until there is a decision “on the appropriate format for the inquiry.”
The main opposition party is calling for an immediate investigation. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Yashar and a candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the conduct of Netanyahu and his circle is “a tangible, direct and immediate threat to Israeli democracy,” warning that “as long as Netanyahu is in office, there will be no more fair and proper elections in Israel.”
Israel faces political chaos as Netanyahu’s grip on power weakens. What will it take to end the disarray?
Two Arab parties that saw record voter turnout in the elections also demanded an immediate criminal investigation.
“The arrest of our activists in the Negev on the morning of the elections and the attempt to silence Arab Knesset members, if proven, is a direct attack on the integrity of the elections and the will of the voters,” Raam said in a statement, referring to Israel’s parliament. The Joint List called to establish an independent commission of inquiry – the state’s highest investigative body – and suspend all involved police and Shin Bet officials.
“Netanyahu tried to steal our vote, but our vote is what will bring him down. His place is not in the Prime Minister’s Office, but in the interrogation room and before the court,” the party said in a statement.
Since losing his parliamentary majority in the October 27 vote, Netanyahu and his allies have raised various allegations against the Arab parties, accusing them of bribery, foreign funding, and fraud. David Zini, the director of the Shin Bet domestic security service and a Netanyahu loyalist, has pressed to investigate Arab politicians over allegations of foreign interference, but so far hasn’t presented any public evidence to support the allegations against them. According to the Channel 12 report, Zini demanded to wiretap five Arab lawmakers before election day.
The request was refused at the last minute by the attorney general because he did not present any evidence to back his request, Channel 12 reported.
In a statement, the Shin Bet said it carried out “various activities in accordance with its powers under the law.”
Avigdor Liberman, the leader of the Yisrael Beitenu party and the interim chair of the crucial Knesset Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee, said on Monday that he would summon the Shin Bet and police chiefs to discuss alleged foreign interference attempts in the election.

articles.title_orig: NC utilities commissioner resigns days after Duke Energy rate hike decisions
articles.title_zh: NC utilities commissioner resigns days after Duke Energy rate hike decisions
articles.content_orig:
A North Carolina utilities commissioner who pushed for lower shareholder returns for Duke Energy and stronger protections against data center costs is stepping down.
State Treasurer Brad Briner announced Wednesday that he accepted the resignation of Donald van der Vaart, effective Jan. 1, 2027, the same day Duke's newly approved rate increases and utility merger take effect.
Van der Vaart is leaving four and a half years before his term was scheduled to expire. The announcement did not provide a reason for his departure.
“I appreciate Don’s willingness to serve on the Utilities Commission and wish him the best,” Briner said in a statement.
Van der Vaart did not participate in Monday's Duke Energy Carolinas rate decision and issued a partial dissent in the Duke Energy Progress case.
He was also unable to participate in the commission's decision on Duke's long-term energy plan after missing evidentiary hearings while on vacation.
In his partial dissent, van der Vaart advocated for a lower return on shareholder equity than the approved 9.8% and raised concerns about residential customers being left to pay for power plants that could outlast data center contracts by decades.
The commission approved residential rate increases of roughly 9% over two years, along with new financial requirements for large energy users intended to protect other customers from shouldering their costs.
Van der Vaart joined the commission in April 2025 after being nominated by Briner, a Republican.
Republican lawmakers previously changed the commission's appointment structure, reducing its membership from seven to five and shifting appointment power away from the governor.
His departure opens a seat on the commission just weeks before Democrats are set to take control of the state House.
Briner said he would announce an appointment to fill the vacancy in the coming days or weeks.
Van der Vaart, an engineer and attorney, previously served as secretary of the N.C. Department of Environmental Quality and on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Scientific Advisory Board.

articles.title_orig: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
articles.title_zh: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
The disgraced comedian is in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Andy Burnham's official spokesperson said the prime minister believed "the public have heard enough from Russell Brand", and his victims "now deserve peace from him".
Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."
On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be taken down, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed, adding that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
Asked if the YouTube channel should be taken down, the prime minister's spokesperson said: "We hope and trust they will do the right thing."
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.
The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with Google.
Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".
"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".
Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" that the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".
Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".
"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.
Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.
Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".
Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.
In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told the Today programme this week.
She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.
"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."
The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.
Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.
"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."
Additional reporting by Steven McIntosh and political correspondent Harry Farley

articles.title_orig: Trump: ‘We spy on China, they spy on us’
articles.title_zh: Trump: ‘We spy on China, they spy on us’
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

Before joining The Times, Wilner was chief Washington correspondent for McClatchy, where his enterprise and international reporting was recognized with multiple awards. articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump, right, Chinese President Xi Jinping, center, and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China. Win McNamee/Pool photo via AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China and MOSCOW, Russia — President Trump joined Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for a trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China on Thursday – capping two days of talks characterized by high-minded tributes to the role of great powers in maintaining peace, even as the men who led them had a role in starting some of the most intractable conflicts around the globe.
"History tells us when great powers are at peace, the world is secure," said Xi in opening remarks before cameras. "When great powers clash, the world is in chaos."
Putin noted their nations could make a "significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world."
"In that sense and I think in lots of other ways, we are making history," said Trump, who called it a "special responsibility" for the three countries to work together.
Yet, they offered few solutions toward peace, with the leaders offering divergent agendas going in:
Trump wanted to talk about reducing nuclear weapons and his mission to keep Iran from obtaining them; Putin was looking to push for an end to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow; Xi was signaling he hoped to avoid wading too deep into either topic — preferring to showcase China's growing global clout with more general statements promoting peace and economic stability.
There were also topics to avoid: Trump refused to engage with journalists' questions over China's alleged role in an espionage plot to steal high end Nvidia chips.
In the end, the summit's key deliverable was arguably the image itself: the president of the United States gathering with authoritarian leaders from China and Russia for the first time in American history.
Despite being billed as a summit of "groundbreaking significance" by the Chinese hosts, sit-down talks between Trump, Xi, and Putin were relatively brief — with some of that time taken up by interpreters delivering simultaneous translation.
Trump's meeting with Putin lasted 42 minutes. His talks with Xi went about an hour. The trilateral group session went on for an hour and a half.
Still, it was enough time for familiar Trump bonhomie to emerge.
"Who's he? He's my friend," said a smiling Trump upon seeing Putin ahead of their bilateral meeting.
"We've known each other for a long time," added Trump after he and the Russian leader warmly shook hands. "And I think a lot of wonderful things can come of this. Or at least start."
Similarly, Trump told Xi "as long as you and I are in charge of things, we're never going to have a problem."
Both statements were tacit admissions the clock is ticking on Trump's remaining two years in office — with change coming even sooner to Washington when Democrats take control of Congress come January.
The China gathering was first proposed by Putin during an October phone call with Trump — an offer to meet together with President Xi when China hosted the Asian Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) conference in China that November.
For Putin in particular, the meeting was always going to be a coup: the latest sign that — with Trump and Xi's help — he has effectively chipped away at Western attempts to isolate him politically over his invasion of Ukraine.
Back in Moscow, state media showed footage of the three leaders huddled together seemingly on loop — proof that Russia had regained what the Kremlin sees as its rightful place among global superpowers.
Ignored by Kremlin-friendly media were hints at more subtle power dynamics at play.
Xi greeted Trump on the tarmac personally — returning a gesture Trump had given the Chinese leader during his recent visit in Washington — while Putin received a more scaled down delegation upon arrival to Shenzhen.
Similarly, Trump was offered the top spot next to Xi during the APEC group photo and sat next to Xi during the APEC dinner reception — with Putin positioned at a separate table.
Was it a slight to Putin? A calculated attempt to flatter Trump? A reflection of Russia's vastly weaker economy? Whatever the answer, Xi wasn't ignoring his Russian guest entirely.
The two gathered privately for two hours on Wednesday — a sit-down China-Russia watchers estimated to be their 50th meeting all told.
Xi and Putin also echoed each other in their public speeches— both touching on familiar themes of the dawn of a new "multipolar world" and criticizing the use of sanctions as a sign of Western influence on the wane.
From the outset, critics of the summit voiced concern that Trump, Xi, and Putin would seek to carve the world into each country's perceived sphere of influence.
In Russia, the event was billed as a potential "new Yalta" — a reference to a moment in 1945 when the leaders of the U.S., Soviet Union, and United Kingdom hastily agreed to a post-World War II order for Europe.
Instead, the Shenzhen summit reflected the far more fragmented priorities of its participants.
Trump made no secret he hoped to include China in arms control talks — what Trump calls "denuclearization" — at a moment when key landmark nuclear treaties between Russia and the U.S. have all expired.
The catch: his Chinese hosts had little interest in the issue.
Beijing has repeatedly rebuffed U.S. attempts to include it in negotiations with Russia — noting that its arsenal remains far below those of Cold War-era rivals Moscow and Washington.
Differences also extended to the war in Ukraine, where Putin had hoped to press for U.S. and Chinese support for a settlement tilted in Moscow's favor — including a redrawn security map for Europe that would amount to a rollback of NATO from Eastern Europe.
Xi has insisted Europe have a seat at the table in any negotiated settlement. Trump has largely relied on his trusted envoys — real estate developer Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner — to hash out the complexities of any peace deal.
Following Trump's meeting with Putin, a Kremlin aide would only say that Ukraine had been the focus of the discussions — adding the Kremlin leader had left "in an excellent mood."
Just hours earlier, Ukraine carried out a missile strike on the lone bridge linking mainland Russia to the annexed Crimean peninsula for the third time this week — effectively disabling the structure for months to come.
The bridge is widely considered the Russian leader's pet project — a symbol of Russia's claim to territory illegally seized from Ukraine in 2014 rendered in steel.
Additional research by Jasmine Ling.

articles.title_orig: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.title_zh: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.content_orig:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
Automatic gunfire could be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
At least 1,658 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,700 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Risk of US Strikes on Iran Grows as Sides Escalate Skirmishes
articles.title_zh: Risk of US Strikes on Iran Grows as Sides Escalate Skirmishes
articles.content_orig:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian forces have targeted military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait as the United States has hit military and radar installations in southern Iran after a spate of attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Both the US and Iran appear reluctant for all-out conflict again, as happened during the opening weeks of the war, which the US and Israel began on February 28. But analysts said the current situation is inherently unstable and could potentially escalate again into full-blown war that could see Israel rejoin the strikes on Iran.
US forces are deployed at military bases in Bahrain and Kuwait, which Tehran considers complicit in the recent strikes on southern Iran. The two countries had not been attacked since early September, but both have been targeted by Iranian drones in recent days.
The lull for Bahrain ended on November 13 when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) directed explosive-laden drones towards the Riffa Air Base after US air strikes in Sirik, a port on Iran’s Hormozgan coast. Several more Iranian strikes have followed, and the US has also attacked Iran’s Qeshm Island on multiple occasions.
After hitting Bahrain, the IRGC warned Manama against its security partnership with the US and its treatment of Shia Muslim leaders after several were recently given lengthy prison sentences.
Kuwait reported incoming drones overnight into Wednesday. Iran’s military said it was targeting US equipment at Ali Al Salem Air Base, including missile launch platforms. No Iranian missiles were used against Bahrain or Kuwait, unlike attacks earlier in the war, according to reports.
Mohammad Eslami, a Tehran-based foreign policy analyst, said Iran aims to gradually degrade US military assets across the region, particularly those Tehran believes were active during the war.
“So long as the war does not end in a political agreement, Iran will continue to do this, regardless of other factors like the blockade,” he told Al Jazeera.
US President Donald Trump and senior officials in his administration have insisted a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports and tough sanctions against Tehran are working. These appear designed to either force Iran to concede to US demands for ending the war or lead to the collapse of its government.
But Tehran is increasingly signalling that it will not accept a continuation of the status quo as the sanctions are severely impacting imports and exports to Iran. The Iranian military’s targeting of regional military facilities this week is likely related to this US economic embargo, said Andreas Krieg, an associate professor in security studies at King’s College London.
“The strikes on Bahrain and Kuwait are about probing American red lines, testing how far Tehran can push the boundaries of military confrontation without triggering another full-scale war,” Krieg told Al Jazeera.
“By targeting American assets in Gulf states, Iran is trying to make Washington’s economic warfare increasingly costly for its regional partners.”
The US military’s Central Command says its maritime blockade has prevented Iran from loading any crude oil onto its tankers since late August. It has also claimed more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have been shipped through the Strait of Hormuz by Iran’s Arab neighbours under US protection and in defiance of demands for vessels to use a route Tehran has authorised.
Iran continues to sell oil stored outside the blockade limits to China, although at reduced levels.
The IRGC maintains that the strait remains closed to unauthorised transit and continues to target the oil shuttle system, which it believes is run primarily by the United Arab Emirates . This relay system has succeeded in getting more energy exports out of the Gulf using tankers that transfer their cargoes to other ships that deliver the oil to global markets.
The UAE’s state-owned Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) confirmed on Wednesday that one of its vessels was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz and one crew member was missing.
To reopen the strategic waterway, Tehran has demanded the US lift its blockade and an Iran-Oman deal outlining coordinated transit routes in the strait be honoured along with other carefully sequenced US concessions on lifting the sanctions on Iran and releasing its frozen assets.
Mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to try to bridge the gaps between the two sides, but the talks have largely reached an impasse as both sides refuse to budge on their main demands.
Eslami said Trump and his senior political and military officials have failed to adopt a clear strategy towards Tehran, particularly in light of Iran’s promise of a response across the region and beyond if attacked.
“The “Iron Gate” and other measures are effectively a pretty name for their indecision,” he said about the US plan to create overland trade disruptions . “The issue in the negotiations is that they don’t know what to do about the raised proposals due to the political costs they would have to pay in the US.”
Still, some Iranians appear to believe they are the dominant party in the current impasse. Speaking to state television on Wednesday, the IRGC’s political deput,y Yadollah Javani, said Trump was stuck in a “quagmire” and must accept defeat.
“Trump has no choice but to accept realities in the field,” he said, adding that Iran was upgrading its arsenal and prepared for another major outbreak in fighting with the US.
After a third US aircraft carrier strike group entered the Arabian Sea, Iran’s army chief, Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were prepared for any new attacks by Washington.
“The enemy is preparing its forces, but the army and other armed forces monitor their movements vigilantly,” he said in a speech on Wednesday. “The preparedness of armed forces increases by the moment. Our response to any error by the enemy and its backers will be more decisive than before.”
Trump’s administration appears split on how to handle Iran with hawks such as Defense Secretary Pete Hesgeth reportedly wanting a more forceful approach to Tehran.
Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, said others believe Washington can maintain the blockade and economic pressure indefinitely while avoiding full-scale war. But the latest attacks demonstrate the difficulty of maintaining such an arrangement.
“Beyond the risk of unintended escalation, the longer the blockade and economic pressure campaigns continue, the greater the incentive for Tehran to deliberately escalate in an attempt to break the deadlock by force,” he wrote in an analysis online.
Krieg said he expects Tehran to intensify calibrated pressure through attacks on US military assets and by continuing to target vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
This strategy could also potentially press the Iran-allied Houthis, the Yemeni armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), to make further advances along the Bab al-Mandeb strait , another strategic chokepoint for maritime trade and global energy supplies.
“But this equilibrium is inherently unstable. If diplomacy fails to produce tangible economic relief, I believe further escalation will become increasingly likely,” Krieg said. “The greatest danger is that both sides keep pushing each other’s thresholds until one crosses a red line neither fully understood.”

articles.title_orig: From tarmac to APEC summit table, Japan's PM cuts a lonely figure
articles.title_zh: From tarmac to APEC summit table, Japan's PM cuts a lonely figure
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan.
At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages.
Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi.
The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
In the leaders' group photo, Takaichi was placed in the back row, off to the side and several places from Xi, who stood alongside Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Beijing sought to downgrade her official status to that of a head of government rather than a head of state," said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst at Eurasia Group.
During Thursday morning's greeting line, Takaichi spent several minutes trying to talk to the Chinese leader without an interpreter present, while most leaders exchanged handshakes and kept walking.
"It has become increasingly difficult for her to engage in formal or even informal conversations with Xi," said Kei Koga, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, who sees Takaichi's intention as to still "project the image that she could still communicate with him despite the ongoing tensions."
At a press briefing Thursday afternoon, Takaichi said Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communique, adding that her leadership has been communicating with Chinese counterparts on rare earth export controls.
Takaichi's subdued reception signaled Beijing's lack of enthusiasm to repair ties with Tokyo, analysts said, potentially prolonging China's curbs on critical mineral exports that have gripped Japanese industries for the past year.
"China's frosty reception of Takaichi shows quite clearly that Beijing is not yet ready to forgive her over her remarks about Taiwan," Chan said, expecting the bilateral relationship to remain strained until Takaichi leaves office.
That could leave Japan grappling with continued restrictions on rare earth supplies from China next year, said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Relations deteriorated sharply after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and warrant a self-defense response.
While the substance broadly aligned with Japan's existing security policy, previous prime ministers had generally avoided stating it so explicitly in a Taiwan scenario.
China reacted angrily and demanded that Takaichi retract the remarks. She has not done so, while stating that the door to dialogue with Beijing remains open, with minimal high-level contact over the past year.
China has since tightened restrictions affecting Japan, including controls on dual-use and rare earth exports with potential military uses. It also discouraged its citizens from traveling to Japan and halted Japanese seafood imports.
Takaichi's visit marked the first trip to China by a Japanese prime minister since Shinzo Abe traveled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.
No formal Takaichi-Xi meeting has been publicly scheduled during her visit. Meanwhile, Xi is expected to join Trump and Putin for a historic trilateral gathering on Thursday, alongside a bilateral meeting with Trump.
Takaichi needs to show a "reflection of what she said about Taiwan a year ago," said Huiyao Wang, founder of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, which is often seen as close to Beijing's thinking.
Wang said Tokyo should show greater flexibility, pointing to Trump's comments that the U.S. would avoid getting involved in the Taiwan issue. He argued that Japan holding firm on the issue would not help relations with Beijing.
Such reflection, he said, "would really help to clarify some of those misunderstandings between the two countries."
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: TSMC and Samsung suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers
articles.title_zh: TSMC and Samsung suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers
articles.content_orig:
A group of 15 national security experts and AI policy leaders is urging the Justice Department to investigate what Nvidia knew about the alleged smuggling of its advanced AI chips to China,  and whether the company continued doing business with customers after evidence emerged that they were illegally diverting the technology.
The letter, sent Tuesday and addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche, asks the DOJ to examine whether Nvidia kept selling chips to customers or middlemen after receiving evidence that they were illegally routing them to China, or whether the company “deliberately blinded itself to export control violations.”
“The United States has the world’s most advanced SI chip technology, much of it built by Nvidia,” the letter states, using the Trump administration’s “super intelligence” label for AI. “Smuggling operations threaten to undermine that lead, giving China access to hardware necessary for developing advanced SI and deploying it to boost its military capabilities and international influence.”
The 15 signatories include a range of national security experts and artificial intelligence policy specialists, such as David Buckley, former CIA inspector general; Randy Manner, a retired Army general; Chris McGuire, a former Biden official who specialized in chips; and Brad Carson, the president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, the AI advocacy group that organized the letter.
“China and our competitors around the world have their sights set on our advanced AI chips so they can build up their AI capabilities,” Carson told NBC News. “Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are at the top of their wish lists.”
Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. On Tuesday, the company’s board of directors announced that it would establish a committee dedicated to investigating national security and export control compliance.
In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson said: “As a general policy, the Department doesn’t discuss the details or existence of ongoing investigations, but it goes without saying that any investigation by the DOJ is based in evidence and facts.”
The letter comes amid growing scrutiny of the American chipmaker and calls from Congress to investigate the extent of Nvidia’s awareness of the chips’ destination and whether the company did anything about potential smuggling.
On Tuesday, the Justice and Commerce departments shared details about their investigation of Megaspeed , the Singapore-based company tied to Alice Huang, who is suspected to be a Chinese intelligence asset with whom former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is alleged to have had an affair. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China.
In a joint statement Tuesday, the agencies said Commerce opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, requested sales records from Nvidia in May 2025 and that Nvidia placed the company on its no-sell list the following month. Commerce investigators also conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed’s facilities with Singaporean law enforcement in June 2025.
A source familiar with the matter said that Nvidia itself is not the target of any existing investigation related to national security.
The Justice Department said it took the lead in the criminal investigation after that enforcement action. The agencies said they would continue working together to pursue any criminal conduct that may have occurred.
Huang has agreed to sit for an interview with several national security-focused House committees on Dec. 1, according to House Republicans. The appearance will focus on the former CEO’s role in “a potential breach of our national security,” according to the lawmakers.
Tuesday’s letter to Blanche points to several smuggling cases the Justice Department has brought in the past year involving Nvidia. In March 2026, prosecutors charged three people in an alleged scheme in which a Southeast Asian intermediary bought roughly $2.5 billion worth of servers containing advanced AI chips. Prosecutors allege at least $510 million worth were illegally sent to China.
“Repeated attempts to route Nvidia chips to China point to a pattern that warrants a closer examination of company practices and how Nvidia responded to repeated alarming discoveries over the past several years regarding the scale of smuggling operations,” the letter states.
Smuggled chips are estimated to equal at least 25% of the chips Chinese AI companies obtained through legal routes — though the actual figure may be far larger. Many Chinese companies, including tech titans Alibaba and Tencent, have reportedly also leased chips from data centers based in Singapore, Malaysia and other southeast Asian countries.
This week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced that it would close that loophole. The department said it would enact a new set of regulations limiting foreign data centers’ ability to rent their chips to Chinese companies and enacting new requirements for chip customers in five southeast Asian countries — including Singapore and Malaysia — in order to receive chips from American companies like Nvidia or AMD.
China criticized the rule. “Such actions run counter to the consensus reached between the two sides, infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, and disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing.
Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips are widely considered the most powerful available. Under current export rules, Nvidia cannot sell its top-tier chips to China, though it can sell older generation chips, from the H200 family, to China with a 25% fee taken by the White House.
The Justice Department established a new body dedicated to cracking down on AI-related crime in early November. This force, called the Super Intelligence Task Force, aims to “ensure that America’s leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct,” according to the Department.
Some lawmakers have clamored for stricter rules on advanced AI chip exports to China. Members of the House’s Select Committee on China have sought to restrict China’s ability to purchase chipmaking equipment and to implement stronger chip-tracking technology — to ensure that chips sent to data centers outside mainland China remain outside of the country.
Tuesday’s letter closes by urging the department “to follow the evidence wherever it leads and pursue appropriate enforcement action where violations are established.”
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.
