The nine hominin teeth from Baxian cave (specimens with prefix PA) and Naxian cave (specimens with prefix NX) represent different tooth positions (NX-A1-123 (a fourth upper premolar, P 4 ), NX-B1-127 and NX-B2-9 (first upper molars, M 1 ), PA1796 (M 2 ), NX-A1-3 (a first lower canine, C 1 ), PA1798 (P 3 ), NX-A2-56 and PA1799 (P 4 ), NX-B2-10 (M 2 ); Fig. 1 and Supplementary Note 1 ). All of the specimens from these two sites exhibit relatively large dimensions, falling within or close to the size distribution range of H. erectus , but also overlapping with non- erectus Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo and Neanderthals ( H. neanderthalensis ), and being in the higher end of the Pleistocene and Holocene modern human ( H. sapiens ) range of variation (Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Dataset 1 ). The two M 1 teeth from Naxian cave (NX-B1-127 and NX-B2-9) are morphologically close to each other and possible antimeres of the same individual.
Among these teeth, eight show a combination of features usually found in H. erectus specimens, such as an asymmetric P 4 crown 24 (NX-A1-123), short upper molar crowns with a square to slightly rhomboidal occlusal outline 24 , 25 , 26 (NX-B1-127 and NX-B2-9), mesial and distal marginal ridges on both lingual and buccal faces of the C 1 crown 26 (NX-A1-3), together with mesial and distal vertical furrows on the buccal side of C 1 , an asymmetric outline of the lower premolars (PA1798, PA1799 and NX-A2-56) with a slightly protruding distolingual corner of the P 3 crown and a developed trigonid basin on the P 4 crown 24 , 27 , a rectangular and short M 2 crown (NX-B2-10) with a complex expression of the protostylid, and a distal M 2 root with two canals 24 . articles.title_orig: Nasdaq-100 futures surge as traders gear up for Anthropic’s highly anticipated debut: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq-100 futures surge as traders gear up for Anthropic’s highly anticipated debut: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures jumped on Wednesday night as investors looked ahead to Anthropic's public trading debut.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 125 points, or 0.3%. S&P 500 futures added 0.5%, and Nasdaq-100 futures surged 1%
Asia-Pacific markets opened mixed Thursday. Japan's Nikkei 225 inched 0.54% higher, while the Topix fell 0.32%. South Korea's markets will open an hour late due to a college entrance exam. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.12%.
In Wednesday's regular U.S. trading, the blue-chip Dow lost more than 560 points, or 1.1%. The broad market S&P 500 fell 0.2%, marking its fifth consecutive losing session and longest slide since June. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%.
Traders are focused on how the company behind Claude performs when it debuts on the Nasdaq Thursday, trading under the ticker "ANT." The artificial intelligence company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the expected range, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC Wednesday.
Anthropic also upsized the offering, selling around 980 million shares, bringing the amount raised to $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.
The market has become more cautious on AI as of late, with investors focusing on whether heavy spending on the build-out will translate into meaningful profits. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) has fallen 11% this month, and embattled AI bellwether Nvidia has dropped 26% while the company grapples with the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang. Shares of neocloud CoreWeave , which had seen its bond yields trade above 16% earlier this month, is also down almost 13% in November alone.
"It'll be an important barometer for investors' AI appetite," Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp, said of Anthropic's IPO. "AI stocks desperately need some wind at their backs, too ... Wall Street needs a sign that investors still believe in the potential for AI beyond already-elevated expectations."
"The challenge in that thesis is that hot IPOs rarely perform well right out of the gate, especially these days, when every company seems to be vying for a limited pool of capital to fund their AI strategy," she said. "While I wouldn't be surprised to see the stock market take cues from Anthropic's performance, I'd caution investors about trying to read the tea leaves from one event too much."
On Thursday, traders will keep an eye out for weekly jobless claims. On the earnings front, Walmart is slated to report in the morning, followed by clothing retailer Gap after the market close.
Asia-Pacific markets opened mixed on Thursday, after Nvidia shares slid on Wall Street overnight.
Japan's Nikkei 225 inched 0.54% higher, while the Topix fell 0.32%. South Korea's markets will open an hour late due to a college entrance exam
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 declined 1.12%.
Asia-Pacific markets appeared set for a subdued open Thursday, following a mixed session on Wall Street overnight that saw Nvidia shares slide.
Futures for Japan's Nikkei 225 in Chicago were at 59,230, compared with the index's previous close of 59,024.28.
Futures for Hong Kong's Hang Seng index last traded at 23,100 compared with the index's last close of 23,294.75.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 1.19% in early trade.
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, above the expected range, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.
The AI company, along with its seven co-founders, reportedly upsized the offering, sellling 979.6 million shares, bringing the amount raised to $81.3 billion and surpassing SpaceX, which held a record IPO in June.
For more, read the full story here .
— Tanaya Macheel, Ashley Capoot, Leslie Picker
U.S. equity futures were near the flat line on Wednesday night.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced 35 points, or 0.07%. S&P 500 futures added 0.1%, as did Nasdaq 100 futures .

articles.title_orig: Dow drops more than 500 points; S&P 500 falls for fifth day as Nvidia sells off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops more than 500 points; S&P 500 falls for fifth day as Nvidia sells off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell on Wednesday as Nvidia shares lost momentum following the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings report.
The 30-stock index shed 561.25 points, or 1.11%, to end at 50,198.17. The S&P 500 lost 0.23% and closed at 7,323.63. It was the fifth consecutive losing session for the broad market index and its longest slide since June. The Nasdaq Composite outperformed and rose 0.42% to 24,429.88.
Shares of Nvidia were 2.9% lower, reversing course from earlier gains after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
The report marked the chipmaker's first since Jensen Huang resigned last week as CEO, a move that came days after he admitted to an affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The company's board chair, Harvey Jones, said at the start of the earnings call that the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as chief executive.
"It's going to be an adjustment, but it's one that the market will work its way through, just as it always has in the past," said Eric Parnell, chief market strategist at Great Valley Advisor Group.
When it comes to the broader artificial intelligence trade, however, Parnell noted that the underlying fundamental challenges, including those related to capital expenditures and debt financing, haven't changed — and might not anytime soon.
"It doesn't take much of a slowdown in earnings growth in the environment that we're in with the AI buildout and the AI spend to take these types of stocks down pretty quickly," he said. "It's this type of volatility that I suspect we're not only going to continue to see but it's likely to increase as we go through 2027 and into 2028."
The Dow was also weighed down by losses in healthcare stocks like UnitedHealth as well as energy name Chevron and industrial giant Caterpillar . UnitedHealth lost 10%, while Chevron and Caterpillar declined almost 4% and more than 2%, respectively.
On Tuesday, the blue-chip index dropped more than 1%, while the S&P 500 notched its lowest closing level since July 29. The Nasdaq shed almost 1% and touched its lowest level since April during the session.
Investors are looking ahead to a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic later this week. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed lower on Wednesday.
The 30-stock index lost 561.25 points, or 1.11%, to close at 50,198.17, while the broad market S&P 500 dipped 0.23% to 7,323.63.
The Nasdaq Composite, however, rose 0.42% to end the day at 24,429.88.
The stock market might not be fully acknowledging the threat China poses to the U.S.'s standing in the artificial intelligence race, according to UBS.
"US AI leadership remains powerful, but we heard that the market may be underestimating Chinese competition and the potential fragmentation of corporate demand," said strategist Reinout De Bock in a Tuesday note.
"The question is not just how quickly AI capex grows, but who will own the infrastructure, control the data and capture the monetization," he added.
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
Read the full story here .
Energy stocks fell alongside oil prices as investors reacted to last week's rise in U.S. crude and fuel inventories , even though tensions between the U.S. and Iran persist.
Shares of ExxonMobil and Chevron each dropped more than 3%, while others like ConocoPhillips and EOG Resources were down more than 2%.
S&P 500 energy was the worst performing sector during the session, falling nearly 3%.
That's as crude oil prices were lower on the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell more than 4% to $82.19 per barrel. International benchmark Brent crude futures slid more than 2% to $90.83 per barrel.
Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.
The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.
″[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Read more .
SpaceX shares are up more than 3% over the last five sessions as of late morning trading Wednesday, while the Nasdaq Composite is down more than 4%. That separation may be a sign of things to come, according to Morgan Stanley.
"As the AI trade diffuses into its next era, we see scope for further decorrelation and a more durable place in investor portfolios," analyst Adam Jonas wrote in a Tuesday note about SpaceX shares.
Two key things lead Jonas to this prediction: revenue from the company's connectivity — Starlink — vertical, the increasing need for SpaceX's Terafab as the U.S. seeks to create a more independent semiconductor supply chain.
However, a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, Elon Musk's other megacap company, creates a ceiling for the former's stock for now, he said. "Most investors we speak with are broadly comfortable with the merits of a potential combination," Jonas wrote, "but put off by the lack of certainty on timing and potential dilution risk."
Anthropic proxies gained ahead of the company's IPO. Here are some of the moves:
Shares of Amazon and Alphabet rallied 2% and nearly 1%, respectively. The two companies are direct proxies for Anthropic, given their independent investments in the AI company. In April, Amazon agreed to invest up to $25 billion in the company. That same month, Google said it plans to invest up to $40 billion in Anthropic , expanding on a longstanding partnership between the two companies.
Broadcom jumped almost 3%. The chipmaker is a major partner of Anthropic, having announced a special purpose vehicle to finance $63 billion in chips and networking products to be leased to Anthropic.
Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.
"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.
Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Board Chairman Says Jensen Huang Isn't Coming Back, but He May Have a Poker Move for the Ages Hiding up His Sleeve
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Board Chairman Says Jensen Huang Isn't Coming Back, but He May Have a Poker Move for the Ages Hiding up His Sleeve
articles.content_orig:
By Adam Spatacco – Nov 18, 2026 at 4:08PM EST
10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›
Although Nvidia ( NVDA -2.90% ) just delivered another incredible earnings report, investors are preoccupied with the unexpected departure of founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang . During the company's earnings call, board chairman Harvey Jones made it clear that Nvidia intends to move forward without its former leader. Jones said the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation and does not intend to reinstate him.
However, Huang may have another way to influence Nvidia's future. According to a recent Reuters report, Nvidia's corporate governance rules grant the former CEO the ability to nominate two candidates for election to the company's board of directors.
At this time, there is no public evidence that Huang intends to exercise that right. Nevertheless, I think Tesla ( TSLA +0.95% ) CEO Elon Musk and CrowdStrike ( CRWD +7.95% ) CEO George Kurtz make two compelling hypothetical candidates. Here's why.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/18/26
Nvidia's definitive proxy statement from May 12, 2026 outlines a shareholder nomination mechanism known as proxy access. Under the company's bylaws, shareholders who have controlled at least 3% of Nvidia's voting power for three consecutive years can nominate candidates for inclusion in its annual proxy materials. The number of candidates is limited to the greater of two directors or 20% of the board.
Huang has maintained ownership above that threshold for more than three years and currently controls approximately 3.5% of Nvidia. Importantly, this authority comes from Huang's position as a qualifying shareholder rather than a special privilege granted with founding Nvidia.
The proxy statement specifies that nominations for Nvidia's 2027 annual shareholder meeting must be submitted between Feb. 24 and March 26, 2027. It is important to note that nominating directors does not guarantee their election. Shareholders still need to vote on the candidates, and nominees must meet Nvidia's independence standards and other governance requirements.
Nevertheless, board composition matters greatly because directors oversee corporate strategy and executive succession planning. If Huang nominates candidates who share his vision for Nvidia's future, they could potentially influence other directors over time.
Image source: Getty Images.
Elon Musk is easily one of the most provocative hypothetical nominees. Musk's companies are major buyers and suppliers within the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure ecosystem. Moreover, his ambitions extend beyond purchasing Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs). Musk's proposed Terafab semiconductor manufacturing initiative underscores his interest in developing new types of compute capacity to support future AI development.
Sitting on Nvidia's board could theoretically give Musk an opportunity to help shape the direction of one of the world's leading AI infrastructure companies. His experience building Tesla and Space Exploration Technologies also brings an unconventional perspective on manufacturing, capital investment, and innovation roadmaps.
However, commercial relationships between Musk's businesses and Nvidia, as well as potential competition with Terafab, would require scrutiny under the company's independence and conflict-of-interest rules.
George Kurtz is a different but equally interesting possibility. His professional relationship with Huang is supported by a strategic partnership between CrowdStrike and Nvidia. In September, Huang joined Kurtz at CrowdStrike's Fal.Con conference to introduce SafeMind, an agentic cybersecurity system incorporating Nvidia's Nemotron technology.
Huang has previously emphasized that cybersecurity will become one of AI's most compute-intensive applications, positioning CrowdStrike as an important partner in Nvidia's expansion beyond AI model training .
Of course, Kurtz's relationship with Nvidia also creates potential conflicts that would need to be evaluated before any nomination. Still, his experience in enterprise software and established working relationship with Huang make him an interesting candidate for a board seat.
Corporate boards are rarely unanimous on every single decision. For this reason, newly elected directors could potentially encourage the board to reconsider a decision that initially appeared final.
However, there are some obstacles to this scenario. Board members have fiduciary obligations to Nvidia and its shareholders. This means they must evaluate strategy and leadership decisions independently rather than simply following the wishes of the shareholder who nominated them.
Timing presents the biggest challenge, because Nvidia could appoint a new CEO well before its 2027 annual meeting. This means that even if Huang nominated two successful candidates, reversing the company's leadership transition would require support from additional directors.
Regardless, Huang's proxy-access provision introduces a governance consideration that investors shouldn't overlook. His substantial ownership still gives him an indirect avenue to influence Nvidia's future, even after resigning. Whether he chooses to exercise that right is not yet known, but even the possibility could keep speculation surrounding his return alive.
For investors, the big-picture issue is whether Nvidia can preserve its innovation, strategic relationships, and competitive advantages established under Huang's tenure. Ultimately, Nvidia's ability to execute its AI strategy under new leadership is more important than the possibility of a dramatic boardroom comeback.

articles.title_zh: ‘An absolute nightmare’ — Trump’s trilateral with Xi and Putin spooks allies
articles.content_orig:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official. The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
Meanwhile, a meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Wednesday. “No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua . Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen , reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace. Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin . In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age. “Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen. World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just ⁠concluded a “very big ⁠trade ​deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila ⁠did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the ⁠biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it ​is a fair ‌deal for both countries,” ‌Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine ‌presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the US public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the US worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
The meeting between the leaders of China , the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
“No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin , Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.
The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.
Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace.
Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
The gift may have gone down particularly well with Trump, who has something of a reputation for his love of fast food. The US president has long been associated with McDonald’s and KFC, with his former campaign aides revealing in 2017 that his usual McDonald’s order included two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and a chocolate milkshake. The Guardian reported on their revelations at the time in this article:
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen.
World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
Sheinbaum, however, flew in economy class from Mexico City to Shenzhen on a China Southern Airlines flight, media reports said. She arrived in China on Monday.
Posts on Chinese social media platform Weibo showed the Mexican leader in the plane chatting with passengers, though the photos could not be independently verified by AFP. A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival in China garnered 10.2m views as of Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Sheinbaum said ​on Wednesday she had a “very good ⁠meeting” with her US counterpart Trump ⁠as the two ​countries ‌pursue negotiations aimed ‌at easing trade tensions.
“We ‌continue to make progress on our shared agenda,” Sheinbaum added in a post on ‌X.
The Canadian prime minister’s office has issued a statement following Mark Carney’s meeting with US president Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.
double quotation mark This evening, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of the United States, Donald J. Trump, on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, in Shenzhen, China.
The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.

articles.title_orig: Michigan Industry Leader Warns of Risks as Canada, China Discuss Auto Trade
articles.title_zh: Michigan Industry Leader Warns of Risks as Canada, China Discuss Auto Trade
articles.content_orig:
U.S.-China commission leaders warn of growing Chinese military capabilities, threats to Taiwan and risks to American security ahead of Trump’s summit with Xi and Putin.
President Donald Trump faces a potentially dangerous "two versus one" negotiating scenario when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, two senior members of a congressional China watchdog warned Wednesday, raising concerns that Beijing could seek concessions on Taiwan while Moscow pushes for greater U.S. pressure on Ukraine.
"I think it is two versus one. We have China and China's junior partner, Russia," Randall Schriver, chairman of the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission, told Fox News Digital in a Zoom interview. "Largely they come to the table as a team versus President Trump and the United States," he said, citing China's support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES
President Donald Trump greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as President Xi Jinping watches, before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa/Pool via Reuters)
The warning comes ahead of Thursday's planned trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China , on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The high-stakes talks are expected to address issues such as the wars in Ukraine and Iran, trade and nuclear weapons.
Mike Kuiken, the commission's vice chairman, echoed Schriver's assessment, arguing that Moscow's growing dependence on Beijing puts Trump at a disadvantage.
"Putin is a client state of Xi Jinping, and that essentially means that President Trump is in the room with a two against one scenario, and the stakes are significant," Kuiken told Fox News Digital.
"China is fueling Russia's war machine in Ukraine, and they are basically the lifeblood of the Russian economy at this point," he added.
TRUMP TO CONFRONT XI AT HIGH-STAKES SUMMIT OVER CHINA BACKING FOR IRAN, RUSSIA
Vladimir Putin shakes hands with Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Summit in Shenzhen, China, Nov. 18, 2026. (Sputnik/Sergei Bobylyov/Pool via Reuters)
The commissioners spoke as the bipartisan body released its 2026 annual report to Congress , detailing Beijing's expanding military, technological and economic capabilities and the growing challenges they pose to American national security.
Asked what would constitute success or failure at the summit, Kuiken suggested Beijing would not have agreed to the meeting without assurances that its interests would be protected.
"My assessment is that the Chinese would never have agreed to this meeting if they had not had significant assurances that essentially nothing would happen," Kuiken said.
Schriver warned that both Xi and Putin would seek opportunities to advance their strategic objectives. He suggested Beijing would pursue gains related to Taiwan, while Moscow would hope Trump emerged from the meeting prepared to increase pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
CHINA'S XI SURPRISES TRUMP AT TARMAC, RECIPROCATING GESTURE SHOWN MONTHS AGO
President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping meet at the Great Hall of the People on May 14, 2026, in Beijing, China. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)
"If Putin had his way, Trump would emerge from the meeting and put more pressure on Zelenskyy," Schriver said.
He also questioned whether sufficient diplomatic groundwork had been laid for meaningful nuclear arms control discussions, one of the issues Trump has indicated he wants to address.
"President Trump would like to talk about nuclear disarmament, probably an agenda that makes sense. I'm just not sure we've done the front-end work when it comes to interagency work, bilateral or trilateral work, at a lower level to have a productive discussion there," Schriver said.
Nevertheless, Schriver suggested that avoiding concessions could itself represent a successful outcome for Washington.
"I think holding ground and just a restatement of U.S. interests is probably a victory of sorts for us," he said.
CHINA’S IRAN TIES COMPLICATE TRUMP-XI SUMMIT AS TENSIONS TEST US LEVERAGE
The Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) fabrication plant in Phoenix, Arizona, on March 3, 2025. (Rebecca Noble/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Beyond the summit, the commissioners warned that the United States faces mounting challenges as China approaches 2027, the benchmark year associated with Xi's directive for the People's Liberation Army to develop the capability to conduct a Taiwan military operation.
Asked whether Washington was doing enough to deter Chinese military action against the self-governing island, Schriver gave a blunt assessment.
"I think the short answer is no, we're not doing enough," he said.
Schriver pointed to a pause in congressional notifications for U.S. arms sales to Taiwan , saying the commission wants those notifications to proceed and supports stronger security assistance for the island.
He also warned that Beijing's increasingly sophisticated coercion tactics extend beyond conventional military operations to include actions involving its coast guard.
"We do talk about counter coercion capabilities and blending not only military capabilities but law enforcement that the Chinese are doing, this sort of blended lawfare with their coast guard east of Taiwan," Schriver said.
Taiwanese conscripts during a visit by Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te to a military base in Taichung on June 28, 2024. (Sam YehAFP via Getty Images)
"It's a tough challenge as we're entering the benchmark year that Xi Jinping said of 2027. There should be more attention to this and there should be greater efforts to this."
Kuiken emphasized Taiwan's importance to the global technology supply chain, particularly its role in manufacturing advanced semiconductors used in artificial intelligence.
"Taiwan is the island at the center of the world. Xi Jinping is obsessed with it," he said.
Pointing to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, or TSMC, Kuiken warned of the broader implications for American technological leadership if Beijing were to take military action against the island.
He urged Washington and its partners to develop a coordinated strategy to make an invasion or other Chinese coercive measures against Taiwan unattractive to Beijing.
President Donald Trump meets with delegations from Japan, India and Australia at the Solaire Hotel, on Nov. 17, 2026, in Manila, Philippines. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Responding to concerns about Taiwan , a U.S. official told Fox News Digital, "There is no change to our policy with respect to Taiwan." Asked about the commissioners’ warnings, a White House official emphasized President Trump’s diplomatic approach to China and his plans to discuss nuclear arms reduction during the trilateral summit.
"Under President Trump’s leadership, U.S.-China relations have been refocused on what matters most – rebuilding the safety, security and prosperity of Americans. And as President Trump has said: much has been, and will be, accomplished, between the two leaders," the official said.
"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People’s Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation."
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," the official added.
TRUMP’S TAIWAN ‘NEGOTIATING CHIP’ REMARK SPARKS ALARM OVER HOW FAR HE'D SHIFT US-CHINA POLICY
A procession of Taiwanese armed military vehicles patrols outside the Songshan Airport in the capital city following China’s announcement of the military exercise Joint Sword-2024B that encircles Taiwan, Oct. 14, 2024, in Taipei, Taiwan. (Daniel

articles.title_orig: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.title_zh: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.
The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.
"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.
"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.
The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."
"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."
Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.
"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."
The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.
But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.
Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.
"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.
A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."
"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.
"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.
"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."
They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.
The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.title_zh: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
articles.content_orig:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission , external .
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
Hundreds of thousands of Rohingya fled across the Myanmar border in 2017 as attacks on them grew
The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.
Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".
A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.
As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.
Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.
It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.
This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.
Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.
Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, was responsible for the military's operations in 2017
The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.
She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.
Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.
Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.
Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.
When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.
Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.
Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.
Aung San Suu Kyi's refusal to condemn the Myanmar military's actions in Rakhine State dismayed her admirers
But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.
"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.
"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."
What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?
Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.
That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.
There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.
The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.
Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar mark the ninth anniversary of their exodus from Myanmar
But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.
"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.
"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."
He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.
More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.
But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.
Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

articles.title_orig: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.title_zh: Fed Officials Saw Higher Rates Ahead When They Held Steady Last Month
articles.content_orig:
Federal Reserve officials expressed confidence in October that further interest rate increases will be needed to stem inflation, though they decided to hold off while gathering more information, according to meeting minutes released Wednesday.
Policymakers put artificial intelligence at the core of their discussions, indicating that demand associated with the technology would be "a material source of inflation risk."
More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.
Those voting in favor of the hold "pointed to benefits in accumulating additional information, which would help in determining the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Since the meeting, the inflation data has shown that the pace of price increases remains well above target.
The consumer price index in October rose 0.4% for all items and 0.3% for the core that excludes food and energy. Both readings were 0.1 percentage point higher than expected.
While indicating concern over how stubborn inflation has been, most Fed officials who have spoken publicly advocated a patient approach.
However, Waller said Wednesday that the Fed may have to "shock" markets by approving a half-point hike in December. He is the only central banker to espouse that belief publicly, though St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said he anticipates as much as a full percentage point move higher by the spring of 2027. As governor, Waller is a permanent FOMC voter; Musalem will not vote until 2028.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said Friday on CNBC that the central bank risks losing its credibility if it doesn't act.
At the core of policymakers' concern is whether rising prices related to the Iran war and President Donald Trump 's tariffs, in many cases temporary events that wouldn't prompt a response, are instead becoming more entrenched.

More broadly, officials said "inflation pressures in the economy were broad based" and would warrant action, with "some" policymakers advocating for a quarter percentage point hike at the meeting. A couple of participants even noted the possibility that a larger increase might be needed at the next policy meeting in December.
The meeting summary said "almost all participants judged that, under their baseline outlooks for inflation and the labor market, further action to raise the target range for the federal funds rate … would likely be appropriate, in order to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent objective."
In a CNBC interview Wednesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller reiterated his belief that the Federal Open Market Committee should consider a half-point hike in December.
Officials at the meeting expressed a high level of concern over AI, both as a source of inflation and financial instability.
Fed staff members who briefed participants noted "that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint."
"Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures," the minutes said. "A few participants remarked that AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms."
Officials said they still expect inflation to fall off sharply in 2027 and beyond as the impact from the current shocks wear off.
Ultimately, the FOMC voted 10-2 to keep its benchmark overnight borrowing rate locked in a range between 3.75%-4%. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase.

articles.title_orig: Ford ships first battery cells using CATL technology
articles.title_zh: Ford ships first battery cells using CATL technology
articles.content_orig:
MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.
The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck , which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.
The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.
The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.
Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.
"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."
The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.
Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.
Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.
Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.
The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

Prince Harry is forcing himself back into the royal limelight with headline-grabbing antics in a war-torn country, a top royal journalist alleges.
As his popularity continues to wane back home, the Duke of Sussex made a surprise visit Sunday to the Superhuman Center rehabilitation clinic in Lviv, Ukraine, where he fraternized with injured soldiers and assured them they will âwinâ the war with Russia.
âEvery single time I come back to Ukraine, I feel welcome, I feel warmth. Youâre going to win the war, and then youâre going to be set up for success,â Harry said at the event.
Harry told Ukrainian soldiers that the United Kingdom has their back.
Efrem Lukatsky/Efrem Lukatsky/via REUTERS
However, former Page Six deputy editor and news commentator Paula Froelich tells The Royalist that she believes the highly publicized trip was another case of Harryâs âattention dependency disorder,â rather than a gesture of actual goodwill.
âIf he doesnât get a headline or heâs not in the paper at least three or four times a week, the poor guy starts to fade away like heâs invisible and doesnât know what to do,â Froelich said. âYou got plenty of veterans at home who need your help, and he ainât paying attention to them.â
Harryâs trip to the east also coincided with Prince William and Princess Catherineâs trip to Mumbai, India, for the Earthshot Prize Awards, a global initiative founded by the next-in-line that awards winners prizes around $1.3 million dollars to bolster environmental solutions.
William and Catherine attended the Earthshot Awards in Mumbai, India on Sunday.
Phil Noble/Phil Noble/REUTERS
âTo put yourself in a position where it looks like you are trying to steal the thunder from an environmental NGOâ¦ just seems so incredibly crass,â The Royalist host Tom Sykes said. âIt just feels like a sort of angry child stamping their feet and going, âLook at me, look at me, look at me,â doesnât it?â
In the public eye, Harryâs friends have maintained that there is no estrangement between him and King Charles. The Sussex couple recently announced that theyâd be staying in England over the holidays, but Sykes suggested it may have something to do with Meghanâs father, Thomas Markle Sr., being arrested in Florida on child pornography charges.
Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, has been arrested on child pornography charges in Florida.
Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Pinellas County Sheriff's Office/Handout/via REUTERS
âNow theyâre saying theyâre staying here,â Sykes said. âPeople canât help thinking itâs not completely unconnected to developments in Meghanâs family, specifically the orange jumpsuit that her father was photographed wearing the other day.â
In the wake of revelations about her father, Sykes said Meghan has appeared âhauntedâ by her lack of control over the narrative.
âSomething has obviously really massively changed,â Sykes said. âShe looks genuinely like not in control of the situationâ¦ And now weâve got sort of Harry trying to pretend itâs business as usual.â
Froelich said that she was surprised to see such emotional imagery of Meghan, considering she has reportedly known about her fatherâs situation for the last several years.
âSheâs leaning into the role of grief store in chief,â Froelich said. âHeâs leaning into the role of âIâve got your back, soldiers,â when, of course, he only really has his own back.â

articles.title_orig: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.title_zh: One of AI's most notorious 'doomers' stands to make billions in Anthropic's IPO
articles.content_orig:
An Estonian tech billionaire famous for his stance that AI could end humanity is expected to be one of the biggest winners in Anthropic's upcoming IPO .
Jaan Tallinn co-founded Skype and later sold it to eBay . He led Anthropic's first funding round, a $124 million Series A, five years ago — well before the company's Claude chatbot was on the market and took Wall Street and Silicon Valley by storm.
Anthropic is set to list on the Nasdaq Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT in what could be the largest IPO of all time, and the first public debut for an AI lab.
Tallinn's exact holdings haven't been disclosed. But given Anthropic's expected debut valuation of roughly $1.4 trillion, the return on his initial investment could be well into the tens of billions. His exact return would depend on the level of dilution in subsequent funding rounds and whether he sold any shares along the way.
Anthropic's earliest backers connected with the company through philanthropic circles worried about AI's existential risk. They're sometimes described as "doomers."
In 2020, Tallinn told CNBC that there's a 1-in-6 chance that humans won't survive this century, referencing a book from Oxford professor Toby Ord. Tallinn also described a runaway AI scenario where a model is left working overnight and "the world is no longer there in the morning."
While he continued to work in tech, Tallinn co-founded the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk and the Future of Life Institute , known for one of the first public calls to pause AI. Despite high-profile signatories , including Elon Musk and Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, the institute's "Pause Giant AI Experiments" letter in 2023 had little effect on the industry.
Tallinn's view on AI was influenced by researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who co-authored the 2025 book "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies," about the catastrophic risk of AI without proper checks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Tallinn, who has an estimated net worth of more than $10 billion, later crossed paths with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who had defected from OpenAI with his eventual co-founders, citing views that Sam Altman's company wasn't taking AI safety seriously enough.
Amodei and Tallinn overlapped in the effective altruism community, according to people who know both of them. Effective altruism, sometimes known as EA , is a philosophy that aims to use data and evidence to maximize philanthropic impact. While there's no official membership, its Silicon Valley network ended up generating much of Anthropic's early venture capital money, according to multiple people.
Tallinn's early bet was that bankrolling a safety-conscious AI company was one of the best ways to keep a lid on the risk, these people said. Tallinn also invested in DeepMind, which was later acquired by Google .
One person, who asked not to be named, said that at the time of Tallinn's investment, there was no expectation that Anthropic "would be a profitable undertaking." Venture investors hadn't yet gone all-in on AI, and it was "before the era of putting AI in your pitch deck," said the person, who asked not to be named in order to speak candidly on the matter.
Tallinn declined to be interviewed for this story.
Anthropic's first round in 2021 also included Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz, who founded Open Philanthropy — now known as Coefficient Giving — which is deeply rooted in effective altruism. The charity was co-founded by Holden Karnofsky, husband of Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei. Karnofsky also started GiveWell, also largely tied to effective altruism.
Former FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried, another known effective altruist, backed Anthropic in its early days alongside Tallinn. Bankman-Fried participated in the Series B in 2022 through his now-defunct hedge fund Alameda Research. The former CEO was convicted of fraud in 2023 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. His stake was sold in bankruptcy auction at a fraction of the company's current valuation.
Tallinn's early investment initially put Anthropic's price tag at $461 million, according to Pitchbook. It has ballooned in value since, and last raised money at a $965 billion valuation in private markets. The lab has raised money from tech giants Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Nvidia, and plans to sell $26 billion worth of shares to a group of tech companies at the IPO price.
Anthropic's early investors and some in the safety community aren't overwhelmingly cheering the IPO. Many worry behind the scenes that AI safety will take a back seat to Anthropic's commercial success and wider shareholder base, according to a person close to the group.
Many in the AI safety community "are opposed to the IPO," this person said.
Others point to Anthropic's unique corporate structure that gives the founders broad discretion and control of the company through a single super-voting share. The co-founders will be sole members of "Founder LLC," which will hold 50.1% of the voting power. But Anthropic is also built as a public benefit corporation, meaning it has a dual mandate beyond just a duty to shareholders. It has to serve the best interests of its "company purpose" to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

articles.title_orig: Brookings’ Michael O’Hanlon on China trip: I hope Trump holds the line on chips
articles.title_zh: Brookings’ Michael O’Hanlon on China trip: I hope Trump holds the line on chips
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.
